metadata.project: King Follett Discourse — digital critical edition
metadata.description: A systematic critical apparatus of the King Follett Discourse, built section by section in Phase 2b (September 2026) against the reading rendering of every witness. It replaces the thirty-four hand-picked variants of January 2026, which were collected without stated criteria and whose readings were paraphrases rather than quotations. All thirty-four ids are kept and revised; new entries run from V035 and are numbered in the order they were added, not in discourse order. Entries are ordered by section, then by order within the section.
metadata.supersedes: the January 2026 collation carried forward in Phase 1

T.name: Times and Seasons 5:15 (15 Aug. 1844)
T.role: Not a report. The composite Thomas Bullock assembled from his own notes and William Clayton's between 23 and 26 April 1844. Recorded in every entry so that the received text can be seen being made, but its agreement with B or C is not corroboration: it is B and C, edited. T is never evidence for what was spoken.

metadata.apparatus_format: lemma ] B reading ; W reading ; R reading ; C reading ‖ T reading. 'om.' = the witness has no counterpart at that point. Printed by `python3 -m kf apparatus Sxx`.

criteria.record_when: Record a variant when, at the same point of the discourse, the witnesses differ in a way that changes the doctrinal claim, the historical detail, the rhetorical framing, or the evidence of what was heard.

types.theological: The variant changes the doctrinal claim, its scope, or its modal force (e.g. 'immortal' vs 'coequal'; 'world' vs 'worlds'; 'God' vs 'Gods'; 'suppose' vs a declarative).
types.historical: The variant changes a factual detail, a name, a number, a scripture cited, or an event.
types.rhetorical: An image, metaphor or framing device is present in some witnesses and absent or different in others (the ladder, the ring, the sun).
types.unique: Substantive content stands in exactly one eyewitness; the others are recorded as om.
types.omission: A passage present in two or more eyewitnesses is lacking in another witness that is present at that point, and the omission is more than a scribe's compression. The entry must say why.
types.reception: T only. T's reading differs from all four eyewitnesses, or picks one eyewitness against the others, in a way that shaped the received text. Typed separately so it is never confused with eyewitness variation. Where T's behaviour at a locus is only one facet of an eyewitness variant, it is recorded in that entry's T reading instead of getting an entry of its own; a reception entry is made only where T's own reading is the thing to be recorded.
types.scribal: A cancellation or an insertion in one report bears on the sense. The cancelled reading is quoted in that witness's reading as 'kept text (canc. cancelled text)'; where a scribe struck more than one span at the point, they are separated by '; '.

do_not_record: spelling, abbreviation, punctuation and capitalisation, except where JSP itself flags them or where they carry sense, in which case the entry says why
synonym-level substitution or word order with no change of sense
a witness merely being shorter, unless the omission criterion is met

fields.id: Stable identifier. V001–V034 are the January 2026 entries, kept under their original ids.
fields.section: The data/sections.json id the variant falls in.
fields.order: Position of the entry within its section, counting from 1 in the order of the base text.
fields.type: One of the criteria types above.

status.revised: One of the original thirty-four, re-examined against the Phase 1 reading text; lemma, readings and significance rewritten where the old entry was imprecise.
status.withdrawn: An original entry judged not to meet the criteria. The id and a reason are kept; nothing is deleted. No entry carries this status at present.

fields.lemma: The base text's words at the point of variation, verbatim from the reading rendering.
fields.lemma_witness: Present only where the base text has no counterpart, and naming the witness the lemma is quoted from instead. Absent means B.
fields.readings: One reading per witness B W R C T, verbatim from that witness's reading rendering, or 'om.' where the witness has no counterpart at that point. For T, 'om.' means T has no counterpart at all, not merely a different one.
fields.reading_sections: Present only where a witness's counterpart falls in a different section from the entry's, because that witness takes the material out of the base text's order. Maps siglum to the section its reading is quoted from.
fields.significance: One to three sentences on what the difference could mean. Hedged by policy: the apparatus says what a reading could show, not what it proves.
fields.jsp_footnotes: The JSP editorial footnotes bearing on the entry, as {witness, n}.
fields.sources: Citations supporting the entry. 'Smith, p. NN' is William V. Smith, The King Follett Sermon: A Biography (BCC Press, 2023), verified page by page against the full text. 'JSP X n. N' is a Joseph Smith Papers editorial footnote.
fields.legacy_verification: Carried forward unchanged where the January 2026 pass left one. It records an examination of JSP manuscript scans no longer held in this repository and is history, not evidence.

metadata.note_on_T: Unlike the Phase 1 file, every entry carries a T reading. T is labelled derived everywhere and is not counted as a collation witness: it is included so a reader can see which eyewitness the received text followed at each point, and where it followed none.

variants.lemma: who was crushed to death in a well

readings.B: who was crushed to death in a well
readings.W: who was crushed to death in a well
readings.R: who was crushed in a well. by the falling of a tub of rock on him
readings.C: who was crushed to death &c—
readings.T: who was crushed to death in a well

variants.significance: Richards alone records the physical cause of death, a falling tub of rock; Clayton breaks off at '&c—' and does not name the well. The difference is one of reportorial fullness rather than doctrine, but it is the only place in the discourse where the occasion's factual detail varies, and T, drawn from Bullock and Clayton, preserves neither Richards's detail nor Clayton's ellipsis.

variants.lemma: I have ben requested to speak by his friends & relatives

readings.B: om.
readings.W: om.
readings.C: I have ben requested to speak by his friends & relatives
readings.T: I have been requested to speak by his friends and relatives

variants.significance: Clayton alone records that Joseph Smith was speaking at the family's request rather than on his own initiative. If accurate it locates the discourse as a commissioned funeral sermon; Bullock's opening presents it instead as a subject the speaker has chosen. T takes Clayton's clause into the received text.

variants.lemma: faith the instruction. of Almighty God

readings.B: faith the instruction. of Almighty God
readings.W: I want the Prayers & faith of the Saints that I may have the Holy Ghost
readings.C: want your prayers faith, the inspiration of Almighty God, the Gift of H. G.
readings.T: I want your prayers and faith, the instruction of Almighty God and the gift of the Holy Ghost

variants.significance: JSP flags Bullock's word as possibly 'inspr.', and Clayton reads 'inspiration'. What is asked for differs: instruction is content delivered, inspiration is a condition of the speaker. Woodruff and Clayton both name the Holy Ghost here, which Bullock does not; T prints both Bullock's 'instruction' and Clayton's gift of the Holy Ghost, so the received text carries a reading no single report supports.

variants.lemma: that it may enter into the ear of the Ld of Sabaoth

readings.B: om.
readings.W: om.
readings.C: that it may enter into the ear of the Ld of Sabaoth
readings.T: that it may enter into the ear of the Lord of Sabaoth

variants.significance: Clayton alone records the allusion to James 5:4. It is a scriptural warrant for the petition Bullock reports in plain terms ('let the prayers of the Saints to heaven appear'), and its presence only in Clayton suggests either that Bullock compressed it or that Clayton supplied a familiar phrase; T keeps it.

variants.lemma: the great Eloe

readings.B: the great Eloe
readings.W: the Eloheem
readings.C: the great Elohem that sits in the h.
readings.T: the great Eloheim, that sits in yonder heavens

variants.significance: The three reports transliterate the divine name differently, and Smith reads Bullock's form as 'Eloi' or 'Eloe'. Transliteration alone would fall below the threshold of this apparatus, but the name is the subject of the sermon's central argument and 'Eloi' would carry an accidental echo of Mark 15:34. Clayton alone locates the Eloheim in the heavens, a clause T adopts and expands to 'yonder heavens'.

variants.lemma: but if we start wrong it is hard to get right

readings.B: but if we start wrong it is hard to get right
readings.W: but if you start wrong you may go wrong.
readings.C: start wrong hard matter to get right.
readings.T: but if we start wrong, it is a hard matter to get right.

variants.significance: Bullock and Clayton report a claim about the difficulty of recovery; Woodruff reports a claim about the risk of error. The modal force differs: 'hard to get right' concedes that a wrong start can be corrected with effort, 'you may go wrong' makes going wrong a contingency rather than a condition to be repaired. Smith identifies the saying as an adaptation of a Lorenzo Dow proverb and notes that Woodruff reports its parts out of the order the other audits give.

variants.lemma: they do not comprehend any thing that is past or that which is to come

readings.B: they do not comprehend any thing that is past or that which is to come
readings.W: they do not know they do not understand their relationship to God
readings.R: If men do not comprehend the character of God they do not comprehend themselves.
readings.C: They cannot comprehend from the beginning no the end not their own relation
readings.T: They do not comprehend any thing, that which is past, or that which is to come

variants.significance: The four reports name four different objects of human ignorance: past and future (B), relationship to God (W), the self (R), and all three together (C). Richards's contrapositive is the strongest form, tying knowledge of God directly to self-knowledge, and Smith observes that it is not equivalent to Clayton's conjunction. JSP flags Clayton's 'no' as possibly 'nor', which would not change the sense. T follows Bullock and drops the self-knowledge claim entirely.

variants.lemma: There can be eternal life on no other prinicple—

readings.B: om.
readings.W: om.
readings.C: There can be eternal life on no other prinicple—
readings.T: there can be eternal life on no other principle.

variants.significance: Clayton alone closes the argument with an exclusivity claim. Bullock, Woodruff and Richards all report the positive form (knowing God is eternal life) and its negative (not knowing God is to lack it) but none reports the further claim that there is no other route. T prints Clayton's sentence, so the received text makes the strongest available version of the claim.

variants.lemma: never say anything against. the man of God

readings.B: never say anything against. the man of God
readings.W: never lift up his hand against me again
readings.R: never lift your voice against the servants of God again.
readings.C: never say any thing against the man of God again
readings.T: never say any thing against the man of God again

variants.significance: Bullock and Clayton report a demand made on behalf of 'the man of God' in the singular, Woodruff a demand made on Joseph Smith's own behalf ('against me'), and Richards a demand extended to 'the servants of God' in the plural. Smith notes that Richards alters the sense. The scope matters in April 1844: the plural would make the claim cover the whole leadership against whom the Nauvoo dissenters were then agitating.

variants.lemma: every man has a right to be a false as well as a true prophet—

readings.B: every man has a right to be a false as well as a true prophet—
readings.W: meddle not with any man for his religion, evry goverment ought to permit evry man to enjoy his religion,
readings.R: Every man has a right to be a false prophet. as well as a true prophet.—
readings.C: no man is authorised to take away life in consequence of their religion all laws and government ought to tolerate whether right or wrong
readings.T: But no man is authorized to take away life in consequence of their religion; which all laws and governments ought to tolerate, right or wrong.

variants.significance: Bullock and Richards report the claim as a right held by the individual, including a right to be wrong; Woodruff and Clayton report it as a duty of government to tolerate. The two are not the same argument, and only the first grants a positive right to false prophecy. Bullock and Richards agreeing on the more striking formulation is some evidence that it was spoken. T carries only the toleration form, so the sharper claim did not enter the received text.

variants.lemma: ninety nine of 100 are false prophets

readings.B: ninety nine of 100 are false prophets
readings.W: om.
readings.C: 99/100 are false teachers
readings.T: ninety-nine out of a hundred are false teachers

variants.significance: Bullock has 'false prophets', Clayton 'false teachers'. The claim's target differs: prophets would indict claimants to revelation, teachers the general ministry. T follows Clayton. Smith records that the later Manuscript History expanded the phrase further, to 'ninety-nine out of every hundred professing religious ministers', without manuscript warrant, so the drift from Bullock's wording continued past T.

variants.lemma: for I speak as one having. authority. & not as a senr.

readings.B: for I speak as one having. authority. & not as a senr.
readings.W: om.
readings.C: I speak in authority—
readings.T: for I speak as one having authority.

variants.significance: Bullock alone carries the second half of the Matthew 7:29 allusion, and JSP flags the last word as possibly 'servt.' while noting the allusion requires 'scribe'. Smith adds that 'senr' might be an abbreviation of senator, which would make the clause a political jab rather than a scriptural one. Bullock himself dropped the phrase when he compiled T, so the received text preserves only the half that Clayton also has.

variants.lemma: who holds this world in its orbit & upholds all things by his power

readings.B: who holds this world in its orbit & upholds all things by his power
readings.W: that holds the worlds
readings.C: who holds this world in its sphere in its orbit— the planets
readings.T: who holds this world in its orbit, and upholds all things by his power

variants.significance: Woodruff's plural 'worlds' extends the claim from this earth to a plurality of worlds, which is the cosmology the sermon goes on to teach; Bullock and Clayton keep the singular. Clayton's 'the planets' and 'in its sphere' are, as Smith observes, premodern images of cosmic maintenance. T follows Bullock, so the received text makes the narrower claim.

legacy_verification.note: Woodruff's 'worlds' (plural) visible with terminal 's'. Bullock/Clayton singular 'world' consistent. Variant genuine.

variants.lemma: If the vail was rent to day

readings.B: om.
readings.W: om.
readings.C: If the vail was rent to day
readings.T: If the vail was rent to-day

variants.significance: Clayton alone frames the vision of God as a rending of the veil, and alone adds 'that is the great secret' just before it. Bullock, Woodruff and Richards all put the seeing in a plain conditional ('if you were to see him to day'). The image makes the claim an unveiling of something hidden rather than a hypothetical, and T adopts both of Clayton's phrases.

variants.lemma: Adam walkd talked & communed. with him as one man talks & communes: with another.

readings.B: Adam walkd talked & communed. with him as one man talks & communes: with another.
readings.W: Adam was made in his image and talked with him, walked with him.
readings.R: Adam was formd in his likeness.——
readings.C: Adam received instruction walked talked as one man with another.
readings.T: Adam received instruction, walked, talked and conversed with him, as one man talkes and communes with another.

variants.significance: Clayton alone has Adam 'received instruction', which makes the exchange didactic; Bullock's 'communed' makes it companionable, and JSP flags his word as possibly 'Comd.' Richards reports only the likeness and no conversation at all. T fuses Clayton's instruction with Bullock's communing.

variants.lemma: I am going to tell you what sort of a being of God

readings.B: I am going to tell you what sort of a being of God
readings.W: I want you to understand God and how he comes to be God
readings.C: Going to tell you how God came to be God.
readings.T: I am going to tell you how God came to be God.

variants.significance: Bullock announces an inquiry into what God is; Woodruff and Clayton announce an account of how God became God. The second is the far stronger thesis, and it is the one the rest of the section argues. T follows Clayton, which is why the received text opens the argument with the becoming rather than the being.

variants.lemma: for he was God from the begin of all Eternity & if I do not refute it

readings.B: for he was God from the begin of all Eternity & if I do not refute it
readings.W: We suppose that God was God from eternity, I will refute that Idea
readings.R: refute the Idea that God was God from all eternity—
readings.C: We have imagined that God was God from all eternity.
readings.T: We have imagined that God was God from all eternity.

variants.significance: Bullock's clause has no attributing verb, so it can be read as an assertion that God was God from eternity or as the opinion about to be refuted; Woodruff's 'We suppose' and Clayton's 'We have imagined' mark it unambiguously as a common belief to be corrected, and Richards's bare 'refute the Idea' agrees. Three witnesses against one on the modal frame make the refutation reading much the likelier, and T prints Clayton's.

legacy_verification.note: All three framing verbs verified: Bullock declarative, Woodruff 'suppose', Clayton 'imagined'. Variant genuine.

variants.lemma: or I will do away or take away the veil so you may see

readings.B: om.
readings.W: or I will do away or take away the veil so you may see
readings.C: om.
readings.T: om.

variants.significance: Woodruff alone reports the alternative Joseph Smith offers to refutation: not argument but disclosure. Smith notes the addition. It casts the whole of what follows as revelation rather than proof, which sits in tension with Bullock's 'I will shew it from the Bible' a few lines later, and no part of it reached T.

variants.lemma: God himself the father of us all dwelt on a Earth same as J C himself did

readings.B: God himself the father of us all dwelt on a Earth same as J C himself did
readings.W: the Father was once on an earth like us
readings.C: he was once as one of us and was on a planet as Jesus was in the flesh
readings.T: God himself; the Father of us all dwelt on an earth the same as Jesus Christ himself did

variants.significance: All three reports have the Father's prior mortality, but they locate it differently: Bullock and T on 'an earth' as Christ was, Woodruff on an earth 'like us', Clayton on 'a planet' and explicitly 'in the flesh'. Clayton's is the most corporeal and, as Smith notes, reflects Nauvoo planetary theology. Smith shows the claim being deduced from John 5:19, and records that the Utah redactors later replaced the whole of it with the Snow couplet.

legacy_verification.note: Clayton's 'planet' clearly legible — distinct from Bullock/Woodruff's 'earth'. Clayton's 'in the flesh' also clear. Three different phrasings confirmed.

variants.lemma: I wish I had the trump of an Arch Angel I cod. tell the story in such a manner that persecution: shod. cease for ever—

readings.B: I wish I had the trump of an Arch Angel I cod. tell the story in such a manner that persecution: shod. cease for ever—
readings.W: And I wish I was in a suitable place to tell it
readings.C: If I have the privilege could tell the story in such a manner as persecution would cease forever—
readings.T: I wish I had the trump of an arch angel, I could tell the story in such a manner that persecution would cease forever;

variants.significance: What the speaker says he lacks differs: an archangel's trumpet (B), a suitable place (W), the privilege (C). Bullock's is an image of amplification, Woodruff's and Clayton's are complaints about circumstance. Only Bullock's reached T. The section boundary falls before this sentence in T, which places it at the end of S09.

variants.lemma: (mark it Br Rigdn )

readings.B: om.
readings.W: om.
readings.C: (mark it Br Rigdn )
readings.T: (mark it elder Rigdon;)

variants.significance: Clayton alone records Joseph Smith turning to Sidney Rigdon by name at the John 5:19 argument. It is the only direct address to a named hearer in the discourse, and it matters for the April 1844 setting, since Rigdon had spoken at length earlier in the conference. T keeps it but raises 'Br' to 'elder'; Smith notes the change of title.

variants.lemma: as the Father. hath power in himself

readings.B: as the Father. hath power in himself
readings.W: As the Father hath power in himself
readings.R: as the father Had power in himself
readings.C: as the father had power in himself (canc. hath)
readings.T: as the Father hath power in himself

variants.significance: Clayton wrote 'hath', struck it, and wrote 'had'; Richards independently has 'Had'. The tense is not indifferent in this sermon: the present tense quotes John 5:19 as it stands, the past tense assimilates the verse to the argument that the Father's work was done in a prior mortality. Clayton's correction is evidence that he heard, or understood, the past. Bullock, Woodruff and T all keep the present.

variants.lemma: you have got to learn how to be a God yourself

readings.B: you have got to learn how to be a God yourself
readings.W: you have got to learn how to make yourselves God, king and priest,
readings.R: you have got to learn how to make yourselves Gods Kings. Priests.—
readings.C: You have got to learn how to be a god yourself in order to save yourself—
readings.T: You have got to learn how to be Gods yourselves;

variants.significance: Bullock and Clayton have 'be', Woodruff and Richards 'make yourselves'; the second makes deification a work performed on oneself rather than a state attained. Richards alone has the plural 'Gods'. Clayton alone supplies the motive, 'in order to save yourself', which subordinates deification to salvation. T pluralises, giving a reading no report has in that exact form.

variants.lemma: & be a King & Priest to God

readings.B: & be a King & Priest to God (canc. God)
readings.W: king and priest,
readings.C: to be priests & Kings
readings.T: to be kings and priests to God,

variants.significance: Bullock first wrote 'be a King & God', struck 'God', and wrote 'Priest to God'. Smith confirms the sequence from the manuscript. What the scribe first heard, or first expected, was the more extreme claim that the hearer would be a king and a God; the correction to 'Priest' brings the phrase back to the Revelation 1:6 formula that Woodruff, Richards and Clayton all report. The cancellation is therefore evidence about what was audible at the point where the sermon is at its most radical.

variants.lemma: from grace to grace until the resurrection.

readings.B: from grace to grace until the resurrection.
readings.W: from a small capacity to a great capacity to the resurrection of the dead,
readings.R: by going from a small to great capacity.
readings.C: from a small degree to another from exaltation to exaltation—
readings.T: from a small degree to another, from grace to grace, from exaltation to exaltation,

variants.significance: Three different metrics for the ascent: grace (B, from John 1:16), capacity (W, R) and exaltation (C). They are not interchangeable — grace is given, capacity is enlarged, exaltation is conferred. T prints all three in a single series, a reading no eyewitness supports and the clearest single instance of its compositive method.

variants.lemma: & sit in everlasting power as they who have gone before

readings.B: & sit in everlasting power as they who have gone before
readings.W: to dwelling in everlasting burnings,
readings.R: Till they are able to dwell in everlasting burning & everlasting power.—
readings.C: till they are able to sit in glory as doth those who sit enthroned.
readings.T: until you are able to sit in glory as doth those who sit enthroned in everlasting power;

variants.significance: Bullock has power, Woodruff burnings, Clayton glory; Richards has burning and power together, which is some evidence that both words were spoken. 'Everlasting burnings' (Isaiah 33:14) recasts fire as the medium of God's dwelling rather than as punishment, and it is the reading that does most theological work. Bullock could not see Woodruff or Richards when he compiled T, and T accordingly prints glory and power without burnings.

legacy_verification.note: Four-way split verified. Richards combining 'burning & everlasting power' suggests JS may have used both words; each scribe caught a different one.

variants.lemma: that all Earthly tabernacles shall be dissolved

readings.B: that all Earthly tabernacles shall be dissolved
readings.W: to know that though they lay down this body it will rise & dwell with everlasting burnings
readings.R: to know their very being will rise to dwell in everlasting burning.—
readings.C: to know that those being shall rise in immortal glory to sorrow die nor suffer any more.
readings.T: although the earthly tabernacle shall be dissolved, that they shall rise in immortal glory, not to sorrow, suffer or die any more,

variants.significance: What is offered as consolation differs. Bullock offers only the dissolution of the body; Woodruff and Richards offer a rising into everlasting burnings, which continues the Isaiah 33 language of the previous section; Clayton offers immortal glory defined negatively, by the end of sorrow, suffering and death. T sets Bullock's dissolution and Clayton's glory side by side and again omits the burnings.

variants.lemma: to inherit the same powers exaltation. until you ascend. the throne of Etl. power same as those who are gone before

readings.B: to inherit the same powers exaltation. until you ascend. the throne of Etl. power same as those who are gone before
readings.W: enjoying the same rise exhaltation & glory untill you arive at the station of a God.
readings.C: to inherit the same glory power & exaltation with those who are gone— before—
readings.T: to inherit the same glory, the same power and the same exaltation, until you ascend the throne of eternal power the same as those who are gone before.

variants.significance: Bullock and Clayton expand Romans 8:17 into shared power, glory and exaltation; Woodruff carries the expansion one step further to 'the station of a God', which names the terminus the others leave implicit. Richards has the bare scriptural phrase and nothing more. T follows Bullock and Clayton, so the explicit statement of the endpoint is not in the received text.

variants.lemma: before worlds came rolled nto existence

readings.B: before worlds came rolled nto existence
readings.W: the same thing as I see the Father do
readings.C: when worlds came into existens
readings.T: when worlds came rolling into existence.

variants.significance: Bullock places the Father's probation before the worlds came into existence, Clayton at the time they did. The difference sets the Father's mortal work either prior to or contemporaneous with creation, which bears directly on how the sermon's chain of Gods is to be ordered. Woodruff has no temporal marker at all. T follows Clayton's 'when'.

variants.lemma: so that he obtains K rolling. upon K.

readings.B: so that he obtains K rolling. upon K.
readings.W: He will take a Higher exhaltation & I will take his place and am also exhalted.
readings.R: god is gratified in salvation Exaltation— of his creations &c—
readings.C: it will exalt his glory and Jesus steps into his tracts
readings.T: so that he obtains kingdom upon kingdom, and it will exalt his glory,

variants.significance: Four models of what the Son's finished work does for the Father. Bullock has accumulation of kingdoms; Woodruff has succession, the Father advancing and the Son taking his place; Clayton has the Father's glory increased; Richards has the Father gratified. JSP flags Richards's word as possibly 'glorified', which would move his reading toward Clayton's. T fuses Bullock and Clayton and leaves the succession out.

legacy_verification.note: Bullock's 'K rolling upon K' visible in shorthand. Four distinct succession models verified.

variants.lemma: it is plain beyond comprehension.

readings.B: it is plain beyond comprehension.
readings.W: om.
readings.C: om.
readings.T: it is plain beyond disputation,

variants.significance: Bullock, the only witness at this point, wrote 'comprehension'; the printed text reads 'disputation'. Smith records the substitution as Bullock's own, made while preparing T. The two are near opposites: 'beyond comprehension' concedes that the doctrine exceeds the hearer, 'beyond disputation' claims it is settled. The received text has the confident reading and the manuscript the diffident one.

variants.lemma: when you climb a ladder you must begin at the bottom rung until you learn the last principle of the Gospel

readings.B: when you climb a ladder you must begin at the bottom rung until you learn the last principle of the Gospel
readings.W: It will take a long time after the grave to understand the whole
readings.R: not all to be comprehended in this world——
readings.C: You have got to find the beginning of the history & go on till you have learned the last— will be a great while before you learn the last.
readings.T: When you climb a ladder, you must begin at the bottom and go on until you learn the last principle;

The effect is to make a general statement about apostasy into a statement about the danger to Joseph Smith, six weeks before Carthage.

T follows Bullock, which gives the received text the most violent of the four in a passage spoken eleven weeks before the killing at Carthage.

readings.T: You never knew my heart; no man knows my history; I cannot tell it. I shall never undertake it;

variants.significance: Bullock and Richards record complementary halves. Bullock has the refusal to tell; Richards has the certainty that the hearers never will know, and the concession that he would not have believed it himself. Richards's 'you never will' is the more absolute claim and his self-doubt the more humane one. T prints Bullock and drops Richards, whom Bullock did not have; the tradition combined them only in 1855–56.

legacy_verification.note: Both readings clearly visible. Bullock: 'you never knew my heart...I shall never undertake it.' Richards: 'You dont know me— you never will...had I not experienced it could not believe it myself.' Both genuine.
